2FA: Monkey Blog PT EN Índice Não Identifica o Dispositivo Quando configuras 2FA em algumas das tuas contas, de cada vez que entras numa plataforma, a mensagem que recebes é «Identifica o teu dispositivo», que envia um código numérico para verificar. Mas a verdade é que o que o código QR ou as chaves de autoridade fazem é identificar o código gerado pela identificação do QR, não o dispositivo. Por isso, se apagares a conta do teu dispositivo e configurares o mesmo dispositivo com a mesma conta, o teu 2FA de autoridade deixa de funcionar, porque não identifica o teu dispositivo, mas aquele código aleatório gerado no momento em que leste o QR. Isto não é segurança, é falsa segurança. Útil, mas falsa. O que o código QR contém na realidade Um segredo, codificado num formato que a aplicação sabe ler. Esse segredo é combinado com a hora atual para produzir seis dígitos, e o mesmo cálculo é repetido no servidor. Se os dois números coincidirem, o início de sessão é aceite. Não há impressão digital do telefone nesse cálculo, nem o nome da pessoa. O código prova que o dispositivo guarda o segredo, não que o dispositivo é teu. Porque é que apagar a conta estraga tudo Quando a conta é removida da aplicação, o segredo é removido com ela. O telefone é o mesmo, o utilizador é o mesmo, o número do SIM é o mesmo, mas aquilo que produzia os seis dígitos desapareceu. Configurar a conta outra vez gera um segredo novo, e o servidor substitui o antigo, e é por isso que os códigos antigos deixam de funcionar. De fora parece um problema de dispositivo. De dentro é um problema de segredo, e a diferença importa: um dispositivo pode ser reconhecido, um segredo só pode ser conhecido. A palavra que o ecrã devia usar «Identifica o teu dispositivo» é uma promessa que o protocolo nunca fez. Identifica um segredo partilhado, que é uma afirmação muito mais pequena, e muito mais honesta. A proteção é real, no sentido em que uma palavra-passe roubada de uma base de dados já não basta, mas é proteção contra uma cópia da palavra-passe, não contra uma pessoa que tem o teu telefone. Útil mas falsa, como diz o título. Continuo a usá-la, porque útil e imperfeita é melhor do que perfeita e ausente. Does Not Identify the Device When you setup 2FA for some of your accounts, everytime you login into some platform, the message you get is "Identify Your Device", which send some numeric code to verify. But the truth is that, what QR code or Authority Keys do, is that they identify the code that was generated by the QR code identification, not the device. So, if you delete your account from your device, and setup the same device with the same account, your Authority 2FA will not work anymore, because it doesn't identify Your device, but that random code generated in the moment you can the QR code. This is not security, this is false security. Useful but false. What the QR code actually contains A secret, encoded in a format that the application knows how to read. That secret is combined with the current time to produce six digits, and the same calculation is repeated on the server. If the two numbers match, the login is accepted. There is no fingerprint of the phone in that calculation, and there is no name of the person. The code proves that the device holds the secret, not that the device is yours. Why deleting the account breaks everything When the account is removed from the application, the secret is removed with it. The phone is the same, the user is the same, the number of the SIM is the same, but the thing that produced the six digits is gone. Setting the account up again generates a new secret, and the server replaces the old one, which is why the old codes no longer work. From the outside this looks like a device problem. From the inside it is a secret problem, and the difference matters: a device can be recognised, a secret can only be known. The word the screen should use "Identify your device" is a promise the protocol never made. It identifies a shared secret, which is a much smaller claim, and a much more honest one. The protection is real, in the sense that a password stolen from a database is not enough anymore, but it is protection against a copy of the password, not against a person who has your phone. Useful but false, as the title says. I still use it, because useful and imperfect is better than perfect and absent.
3wiseMonkeys: Why Refusing to (See, Listen or Speak "Evil") can be positive? 2026-05-24 — — First Lesson: Learn to Deny Orders . Accept suggestions, Accept Critics, Deny Orders! Second Lesson: You are Free . You can make a Choice . Third Lesson: Your Mindset and Your Will to change, is the Key to archive any gold. The image everybody knows and nobody reads Three monkeys, one covering his eyes, one covering his ears, one covering his mouth. The image travels around the world as a decoration, printed on small statues and sold in airports, and almost always it is read as a lesson in obedience: do not see evil, do not hear evil, do not speak evil. Be quiet, be useful, and let the world happen to somebody else. That reading never convinced me. A monkey with his hands over his eyes is not blind, he is choosing. The gesture is active. It says: this, for now, does not enter. And a choice about what enters the mind is the first form of discipline that any person can practice, because attention is the only door we can close without asking permission. To see everything is to be at the mercy of everything A mind that cannot close a door is not open, it is unprotected. The endless feed, the notification, the argument of a stranger at three in the morning, the news that repeats itself every hour with a new face: none of it asks whether we have room for it. It simply arrives, and the mind that says yes to everything ends up owned by everything. So the first monkey is not refusing knowledge. He is refusing noise, which is a different substance. Knowledge has a shape, a source and a reason to exist. Noise has an urgency. Learning to tell them apart takes years and it is the most profitable skill I know. Orders and suggestions are not the same thing A suggestion offers a reason and leaves the decision with me. A critic offers a correction and leaves the decision with me. An order removes the decision, and a person who only follows orders never learns to judge, because judgement is the exact part that was taken away. This is why the first lesson is about refusing without guilt. I am not telling anyone to be rude to a teacher, a parent or a boss. I am saying that the sentence do it because I say so is the sentence that makes a person replaceable. The ability to say no to an order is the same ability that lets someone say no to a bad idea, and a society of people who cannot refuse is a society that can be pointed anywhere by whoever speaks loudest. Accept the suggestion, consider the critic, refuse the order. In that order, every time. Not because authority is always wrong, but because authority without a reason is not authority yet, it is only volume. Freedom is a verb with a price Freedom is not the absence of limits. It is the presence of a choice, which implies that there is more than one path and that the person is the one who walks. Without that, freedom is only a word used in speeches, and the speeches are usually written by people who would prefer that we did not use it. The second monkey covers his ears because some voices are not offering a path, they are offering a direction. A direction comes with a promised reward: the correct opinion, the correct career, the correct life. A path comes with work. The difference is not in the volume of the voice, it is in whether the voice survives the question why . The third monkey, and the gold that is not money The third one covers his mouth, and people read it as silence before injustice. I read it as economy. Words spent on what cannot be changed are words taken from what can. The mouth is not sealed, it is reserved for the sentence that deserves to exist. The gold of the third lesson is not money. It is whatever a person builds when nobody is deciding for him: a habit, a craft, a text, a family, a piece of software, a garden. The mindset is the key, the will is the hand that turns it, and the door opens on the other side of the noise that the three monkeys decided to ignore. How to practice it this week Nothing here works as a theory. It works as a repetition, and it is small enough to start today: Pick one source of noise and close it for seven days. Not forever. Seven days. When someone gives you an order, ask for the reason. If the reason exists, follow it with more will than before. When someone gives you a label, wait a day before accepting it. Labels age badly. Choose one thing to build that nobody asked for, and give it twenty minutes a day. That is the whole discipline. The monkey does not refuse the world. He refuses to be carried by it, and in that small distance between the world and the mind there is room enough for a life. ↑

Where a number is modelled, estimated, or incomplete, this document says so. 00 — Abstract What this document argues, and what it does not This dossier rests on a premise stated plainly: a gun is always a bad tool. That is a moral claim, and no table of figures can prove a moral claim. What the figures can do is something narrower and more useful: they can show what the tool actually produces when it is used, at scale, by every kind of person who uses it. So the document proceeds in two movements. First, an accounting. We count the dead by category — homicide, suicide, accident, police action, war, bombing — and by the hand that held the weapon: a civilian, an officer, a soldier, a child. Second, an argument. From that accounting we ask a practical question: does the weapon solve the problem it was produced to solve? The evidence assembled here says no, and says it consistently enough that the burden of proof has shifted. A third movement follows, because criticism without construction is cheap. If weapons do not solve conflicts between persons, what does? Here the literature is unusually clear and unusually ignored: organised nonviolence outperforms armed struggle by roughly two to one; street-level violence interruption has cut shootings in specific neighbourhoods by double-digit percentages; restorative conferencing measurably reduces repeat offending; purchaser licensing is associated with large reductions in firearm homicide. We report those, including the places where the evidence is weak. A note on intellectual honesty This is an advocacy document built on real data, and it says so. Where a widely-cited claim turned out to be unsupported — gun buybacks, for instance, or the idea that hospital-based violence intervention is a proven fix for adults — the claim is marked as unsupported rather than quietly dropped. An argument that only works when inconvenient evidence is hidden is not an argument. It is advertising. 01 — Method & definitions How the numbers were assembled Four rules governed the collection of every figure in this document. Every number carries its year and its dataset. A death count without a year is not a fact; it is a rumour with a comma in it. "44,447" means nothing until it is labelled CDC/NVSS, 2024, United States . Modelled estimates are labelled as models. The global figures in this document come from the Global Burden of Disease study, which estimates deaths where civil registration is incomplete. They are the best available global figures. They are not censuses, and they carry uncertainty intervals that this document reports. Casualties are not deaths. Bombing datasets usually count people killed and injured. Mixing the two produces inflated headlines, so each table below states which measure it uses. Different datasets are not interchangeable. AttackerCraft: Home Attacker / Craft Security · Attacker loop How an Attacker Works: Debug, Find, Exploit, Vanish Real intrusions start long before the payload fires and end long after: a lab gets built, code gets read forever, bugs get triaged, primitives get proven, payloads get chained to a goal — and then the hard part begins, making every step of it disappear. This page walks the attacker's loop the way an engineer would run it, with the cases that made the loop dangerous in public view. Method note Public write-up level No weaponized code The loop on paper Strip away the mystique and an intrusion is a project with deliverables: access that survives reboots, data that moves, and no evidence it happened. The ATT&CK knowledge base exists precisely because this structure repeats across teams and years — the same tactics done with different tools. A single loop covers nearly every case in the public record: Stage What the attacker actually does ATT&CK tactic Frame the target Read the org from outside: who ships its software, which vendor VPN faces the internet, how stale its edge appliances are Reconnaissance Build the bug Buy one, reuse a leaked one, or mine one from a patch diff Resource Development Get in Through an update pipe, an exposed appliance, a credential, or a wormed service bug Initial Access Turn code into control Prove the primitive, chain it to execution, plant persistence Execution, Persistence Vanish Hollow processes, clear the trail, encrypt the channel, go dormant Defense Evasion The loop, not the line, is the honest picture: defenders push a team back a stage, and the team iterates. NotPetya delivered itself inside a legitimate updater and then spread on its own — delivery and propagation in one stage. SolarWinds sat dormant for months between delivery and execution. The stage table is a map, not a schedule. One thing the loop leaves out, and the law does not: none of this is legal outside written authorization. Systematic intrusion of systems you do not own is a crime almost everywhere — prosecution cases are a search away. The same craft taught by a consent form is ethics in the day job and a charge sheet without one. This page is educational. Techniques appear at the level of public advisories, vendor reports and conference talks. Everything here is knowledge that exists in the open record; nothing here is a tool, a script or a step you can copy to attack a real machine. The workbench Attack engineering starts with an environment where crashing is a result, not an incident. The modern bench is virtual, disposable and instrumented: Disposables. Clone-on-snapshot virtual machines per architecture: Windows 7 through 11, Ubuntu and CentOS LTS tiers, a cast of ARM routers. A clean disk is one revert away, so no crash investigation ever stops at "the target was already dirty". Debuggers on both layers. On Linux: GDB with a enhancement layer for segmentation checks and leak markers. On Windows: WinDbg for kernel work and userland watchers. Reversing-ahead tools like Ghidra see the decompiled forest first; binary diffing against patched builds shows exactly which branches moved. Tracers and process listeners. Procmon on Windows and strace / eBPF tooling on Linux show every file, registry and socket touch — the evidence trail for later "what did the payload actually change" questions. Fuzzers. Coverage-guided engines like AFL++ hammer binaries around the clock; network services get hand-built harnesses that fake the protocol before the socket exists. The lab itself. An isolated network with fake DNS zones, self-signed CAs and a starved supply chain — because a payload that phones home ruins the experiment and the bench. Two habits make this bench work. First, reproducibility: every crash gets a saved VM snapshot, the exact input and a bug title, or the finding evaporates. Second, discipline about the boundary between studying the bug and arming an attack — a workbench that keeps only inputs and artifacts, never weaponized outputs, stays a research tool even if a laptop leaves it. Finding the crack Vulnerabilities surface in three ways: somebody reads the software's own code or cites the patch, fuzzing crashes it, or a third party reports it for sale. All three paths converge on the same artifact: a memory state or a data flow the programmer did not intend. The patterns that repeat Pattern The mistake in one line Where it bites Unbounded copy Buffer taken without checking the length first Network parsers, protocol daemons — EternalBlue lived in an SMBv1 length check Use-after-free Pointer reused after the heap chunk it pointed into was reclaimed Browsers, scripting engines running untrusted content Format string User text passed as a format, so %n writes and %x leaks Gray-haired but still alive in embedded stacks Integer truncation Length sum cast down, so "big" becomes "small" Archive parsers, image codecs TOCTOU race File or socket state checked, then changed before it is used Local privilege edges, kernel cross-namespace work Injection sink Structured input concatenated into SQL, template, path or command language Web applications, admin panels — the MOVEit Transfer SQL injection Deserialization Untrusted bytes revived into an executable object graph Java ecosystems, .NET, Python object stores Logic flaw State machine skips an authorization decision on some path SAML parsers, session-token handling — Citrix Bleed's overread Bug hunting like the professionals Static reading is underrated. A release that ships a security patch hands the whole internet the diff, and the fix commit is an announcement: the changed function, its edge case, and the argument parser that lets it happen. A serious attacker runs that diff the day the advisory drops, reproduces the overflow, and rides the patch cycle behind unpatched servers for weeks. Fuzzing fills in the search the diffs cannot cover. Coverage-guided tools like AFL++ and libFuzzer mutate a corpus, and the crashes that come back are triaged by hand: which crash reaches a fault is easy; which crash reaches a controlled write is the real question. Reading kernel crash callsites, classifying under sanitizer stacks and a boot that survives the fault takes days, and a bug's value is judged at precisely this point — not by whether a stack trace is dramatic. Third is the market. Governments run acquisition programs, brokers sell exclusivity, and some bugs then go silent for years inside a queued exploit. The MSRC advisory for the SMBv1 bug was available for public reading a full month before EternalBlue was burned onto the internet as a worm — the two disclosures, if you line them up on a calendar, are not secret intelligence; they are a patch window that happened to outlast an outlier's patience. Whether you like the ethics or not, the practical lesson survives: your windows are somebody else's bug hunt. Unpatched internet-facing services are the recurring headline-maker in every case file below. Proving the primitive A crash log is not a capability. Before an exploit is worth an hour, the finding is graded: what exactly can the attacker control, and what does that control mean inside the target's memory model? Primitive Meaning Sounds like Info leak Memory the referee never gave you is readable "Session tokens leak from a decompression buffer" — the Citrix Bleed heart Controlled write attacker-chosen bytes can be put at attacker-chosen addresses "Heap overflow with a predictable grooming window" Code execution Arbitrary instructions run in some context "ROP chain lands in user space" Auth bypass The login check is not the memory problem — the logic is "Signed session token replay without MFA" Sandbox escape Code out of the referee's pit, holding real user privileges "v8 to kernel escape in one pivot" The gap between "it crashed" and "I control it" is where most technical effort in this art is spent. A sanitizer-rich build (AddressSanitizer, UBSan, MSan) narrows it: the tooling reports which allocation boundary was crossed, and a heap-grooming sequence turns a wild overflow into a predictable write. Exploitability under a modern OS also has to be argued, not assumed: mitigations like ASLR, DEP, CFI, shadow stacks and MTE all change what a given primitive can become, and the assessment for Windows differs from the one for a router's firmware. Sub-classing matters almost as much. A write primitive anywhere in process memory is far weaker than the same primitive inside a function pointer table. An info leak of one 8-byte slot is weaker than a decompression overread that bleeds kilobytes of token state — the exact delta that made the NetScaler bug into a mass-exploitation event. From primitive to chain The exploit is the primitive plus the payload plus the transport — and the payload is only as good as the chain of mitigations underneath it. This is where theart of "how the application attacks" — building the technique on top of the bug — is at its most technical: Memory corruption chains The canonical chain dates to Phrack's Aleph One: overwritten return address, shellcode in the buffer, done — but that ran on a world without NX. Under DEP + ASLR , the modern combines two ideas. First, a leak defeats ASLR by disclosing module bases. Second, return-oriented programming replaces shellcode with snippets already in the binary — "gadgets" — rethreaded end to end by the controlled stack. The corruption chain ends up as: groom heap → trigger overflow → controlled stack pivot → ROP the call to VirtualProtect (or mprotect ) → payload runs in legitimate memory. None of the bytes you shipped is "code"; all of it is data that happens to steer execution. Web and protocol chains Bug Payload suite Public case SQL injection UNION to dump the schema, then heap the user table, then write a webshell into the app's data — LEMURLOOT on MOVEit MOVEit Transfer / Cl0p (AA23-158A) Buffer overread oracle read of session-token bytes, replay into the admin plane Citrix Bleed / LockBit SSRF Server-side request pointed at the cloud metadata endpoint, harvesting instance credentials a pattern across most cloud-account takeovers Deserialization Gadget chains: no exploit "written" but a chain of ordinary classes waking up each other until the runtime executes Java要对, .NET, Python payload pairs Patch-bypass chain Two minor bugs that each trip an check cancel each other out — bypass some validation a recurring browser sandbox-escape blueprint The chain idea generalizes: the exploit is not the bug; the exploit is the bug embedded in the target's whole context — frameworks around it, cloud behind it, users upstream of it. What makes a bug "high value" is how much context it flings open. The front doors The payload is ready at the bench; delivery is how it meets a real network. Delivery decides most campaigns, and delivery, in every famous case, landed through a legitimate channel — the more trustworthy the channel, the deeper the inevitable detection crisis. Door How it opens Case that burned it Update pipe inside the vendor's build system, so clients install the malware as a routine patch SolarWinds attack: ORION updater shipped SUNBURST USB / air-gap Stuxnet took four Windows zero-days to cross an unreachable network boundary Stuxnet Worm through a service bug MS17-010 EternalBlue on every unpatched SMB server — no interaction needed WannaCry, then NotPetya Managed file transfer SaaS SQL-inject into the channel your vendors already trust MOVEit Transfer / Cl0p Edge appliance session-token leakage on a VPN concentrator Citrix Bleed to LockBit crypto Library everywhere Log4Shell inside the logging library that thousands of apps called for style Log4j / Log4Shell Two lessons sit in the data. First, the front doors are supply-chain-flavored : your least-attacked artifact is usually the third-party dependency your organization forgot it owned. Second, every case gets worse for the defenders because the compromise lifecycle starts before the victim's perimeter — the bug is mined by the attacker weeks earlier, then rides infrastructure you cannot distinguish from the vendor's own. Perimeter defense by itself is structurally behind, as the intrusions cases and the open-range methodology pages both show. Making the attack invisible Once inside, the clock starts. Every write the attack makes is a forensic artifact someone may collect; every network hop is a chance a gateway logs. So the attacker's craft after access is almost entirely defense evasion — and the same loop we walked at the top of the page is the thing being defended against. The exploit is custom-built and discarded An exploit used once and thrown away is silent in every retrospective. When it must be reused, it is armored: randomized packer stubs, per-victim encryption keys, anti-emulation patterns, metamorphic loaders. This is why one attack sample is nearly useless next to a full analysis — 95% of the artifact is a shell around a payload the shell hides. Defense therefore does not match a file hash, but must detect the behaviour the payload implies. The process is wattless Process hollowing (MITRE's T1055): create a legitimate process suspended, unmap its image, overwrite with your payload, resume — the event tree shows explorer.exe , the memory shows the attacker's code. Living off the land : do the work with certutil , msiexec , wmic , PowerShell — tools the operating system itself ships, so the attack "creates" no suspicious binary to match a YARA rule. Fileless behaves : run in LSASS , svchost , or WMI, install persistence as a registry blob rather than a dropped file, so a filesystem scan finds nothing. PPID spoofing / token games : make the malicious child claim a trusted parent, and the process tree looks like the office manager's remote shell. The channels go quiet Command-and-control does not run a hardwired domain. The bibliography shows domain-generation algorithms (a procedure that daily invents new C2 names that only the network design can verify — every server that checks), fast flux, CDN fronting, encrypted DNS. Beacon timing is equally deliberate: long dormancy with randomized jitter beats a naive "call home at the top of every hour" signature. C2 that only phones home when the operator nudges it, as SolarWinds did over 14 silent days, is not a bug in the attacker's infra — it is the design. The trail gets wiped Log clearing (T1070.006), file timestomping, and disabling the service-local security agent are the classic clean-up. The state-level editions go further: encrypting the whole disk, wiping the master boot record, or — in the NotPetya case — overwriting in a way that was not even reversible, so the ransomware-looking artefact doubles as a denial-of-service operation. The exploit is migrating up the stack, from your buffer to your assumptions. Reading the traces back Everything the attacker does leaves a signature, because perfect invisibility is provably impossible at scale — too much state changes in a computer to hide it all from a properly instrumented host. Confirm the event exists, is parsed, and has the fields you need — before writing the rule. Rule. Write it in Sigma, keep it in git, tag it with the ATT&CK technique it covers. Test. CPUHistory: Home CPU / History Science & Engineering · Silicon CPUs from 1985 to Now: x86 and Its Rivals Every machine you have used rests on one stubborn instruction set. This is that line, chip by chip, from the 386 to the hybrid, chiplet, 2-nanometre parts of 2026 — and the two architectures now growing beside it. 6 November 2026 Long read 14 sections What a processor really does A CPU is a loop: fetch the next instruction, decode it, execute it, write the result back, and keep enough state to do the next one in order. Everything else in this article is a way of making that loop run more instructions per second — or of hiding the fact that memory is far slower than the loop itself. Two numbers multiply into throughput. Clock speed is how many cycles arrive each second. Instructions per cycle, or IPC, is how much work the design extracts from each one. A 4 GHz chip at IPC 2 is doing half the work of a 4 GHz chip at IPC 4, and the marketing sheet prints only the first number. The rest of the story is cache : a hierarchy of small, fast memories that keeps the loop fed, from a few tens of kilobytes at L1 to tens of megabytes at L3. The other constant is compatibility. A compiled binary does not care how many cores it has; it cares that the instruction encoding at address 0 is the one it was built for. That single promise is why a line of chips designed for a 16-bit stopgap in 1978 still runs the web browser you are using — and why the alternative architectures have to win on power and price, not on elegance. If you want the other side of the machine, the hardware note and the transistors primer go down to the level below this one. The eras at a glance Transistor counts are per chip, not per package, and the process node is the one the vendor used at launch. Numbers marked with a tilde are rounded. Year Chip Node Transistors What lasted 1985 80386 1.5 µm 275k 32-bit protected mode and paging 1989 80486 1 µm 1.2M Floating point and L1 cache on the same die 1993 Pentium 0.8 µm 3.1M Two integer pipelines: superscalar x86 1995 Pentium Pro 0.35 µm 5.5M Out-of-order execution, L2 in the package 1997 Pentium II 0.35 µm 7.5M MMX and the cartridge era 1999 Pentium III 0.25 µm 9.5M SSE: vector math for the mainstream 2000 Pentium 4 180 nm 42M Deep pipeline, SSE2, later Hyper-Threading 2003 Athlon 64 130 nm 106M x86-64 and the memory controller on-die 2006 Core 2 Duo 65 nm 291M Wide out-of-order at laptop power 2008 Core i7 45 nm 731M Integrated DDR3, SMT, Turbo Boost 2011 Sandy Bridge 32 nm ~1.16B AVX, ring bus, graphics on the same package 2013 Haswell 22 nm ~1.4B AVX2 and fused multiply-add 2015 Skylake 14 nm ~1.75B DDR4, and the long 14 nm pause 2017 Ryzen 7 1800X 14 nm ~4.8B Eight cores and sixteen threads on mainstream AM4 2019 Ryzen 9 3900X 7 nm CCD ~10B Chiplets and PCIe 4 2021 Core i9-12900K Intel 7 — Performance and efficiency cores, DDR5, PCIe 5 2022 Ryzen 7 5800X3D 7 nm — 96 MB of stacked L3 2024 Ryzen 9000 4 nm — Zen 5's wider front end 2024 Arrow Lake, Lunar Lake TSMC N3B class — Tiles, on-package memory, no Hyper-Threading 2025 Apple M5, Snapdragon X2 Elite 3 nm — ARM laptops at 18 cores and 80 TOPS of NPU 2026 Core Ultra Series 3, EPYC 9006 Venice 18A / N2 — Intel's own node ships; Zen 6 goes server-first at 2 nm Twenty-three rows for forty years, and the shape is obvious: capability arrives early, then the industry spends a decade making the same capability cheaper and cooler. Addressing and math The 386 was the machine that made a modern operating system possible on cheap silicon. Protected mode gave the processor four privilege rings, segment limits and page tables, which meant one program could no longer read another's memory by accident or by intent. The 386SX kept the 32-bit core but halved the external bus to 16 bits, which is how a 32-bit computer reached a market still buying 16-bit motherboards. The 486 finished the job by moving the floating-point unit onto the die — until then a separate 387 chip — and adding an 8 KB unified L1 cache and a five-stage pipeline. The clock-doubled DX2 parts (66 MHz internally, 33 MHz bus) were the first mainstream sign that the processor and the rest of the board would stop running at the same speed. That gap is why cache exists, and why the kernel spends so much of its time arranging memory instead of computing. Everything a protected-mode OS does today — separate address spaces, page faults as a signal, kernel and user mode — was specified in that generation. The reason a 2003 processor can still run a 2025 distribution is not nostalgia; it is that the contract was written down and never broken. The clock race From 1993 to 2003, the industry sold frequency. Pentium doubled the integer pipelines and reached 200 MHz; the Pentium Pro added out-of-order execution so the chip could keep working while a cache miss resolved. The famous 1994 FDIV bug — wrong results in the floating-point divider — cost Intel around $475 million in replacements and taught the market to ask what was inside the chip, not only how fast it ran. MMX arrived in 1997 for integer media work, SSE in 1999 for single-precision floating point, and with Pentium 4 the design took a deliberate bet: a very deep pipeline, extremely high clocks, and the assumption that frequency would keep climbing. Willamette launched at 1.4 GHz and the plans ran to 10 GHz. Instead the pipeline stalled on branch mispredictions, the power curve went vertical, and the 90 nm Prescott core arrived at 125 million transistors and 115 watts without a matching jump in performance. Two ideas from that era outlived the architecture. Hyper-Threading, from 2002, exposed two logical processors per core so that a stall in one thread could be filled by another. And dual-core packages, from 2005, admitted the obvious: if single-core frequency cannot rise, ship two of them. The clock race did not end because the physics improved; it ended because the bill for the last few hundred megahertz was heat nobody wanted to cool. Sixty-four bits Intel and HP spent the 1990s on Itanium, a clean-slate design that expected the compiler to schedule instructions explicitly. It shipped in 2001, ran 32-bit x86 code slowly through emulation, and never reached the mainstream. AMD took the opposite route: extend the existing instruction set, keep every 32-bit program working, add sixteen 64-bit registers, and let the operating system choose the mode. That design, x86-64 , shipped in the Athlon 64 in 2003 and Intel adopted it in 2004 under its own marketing name. It is the reason a desktop can address more than 4 GB of memory without a hack, and the reason the 64-bit transition cost users almost nothing: old binaries kept running, new ones got registers and address space. It is also the clearest case in this history of compatibility beating elegance in the market. IPC comes back Core 2 Duo in 2006 was the correction. Built on the mobile work that produced Pentium M, it was wide, out-of-order and efficient, and at 65 nm it beat the previous generation while using less power. Nehalem in 2008 moved the memory controller onto the die, added SMT back, and introduced Turbo Boost — the chip selling its own thermal headroom as extra frequency. Sandy Bridge in 2011 put the ring bus, AVX and a usable integrated GPU on one die; Haswell in 2013 added AVX2 and fused multiply-add; Skylake in 2015 added DDR4 and then stood still. From 2015 to 2020 the mainstream desktop gained a few percent per generation, because the 14 nm node kept being refined instead of replaced. Core counts did move in 2017 — six, then eight — but only after AMD returned with something competitive. The lesson is uncomfortable and consistent: progress follows competition, not the calendar. AMD's long arc AMD spent the 1990s as the cheaper option: K5 in 1995, K6 in 1997, then Athlon in 1999 with three floating-point units and the first mainstream 1 GHz part. Athlon 64 followed with the 64-bit extension and an on-die memory controller, which cut latency for everyone who copied it. Then came the wrong turn. Bulldozer, from 2011, shared the fetch and decode hardware between pairs of integer cores, so an "eight-core" FX part behaved like four modules with weak single-thread performance, and the FX-9590 shipped at 220 watts. AMD lost the desktop for five years and survived on consoles and graphics. Zen, in 2017, was the recovery: a new core with SMT, eight cores and sixteen threads on the mainstream socket, and a large IPC gain over the previous design. Zen 2 in 2019 split the chip into small compute dies on the leading node and a separate I/O die on a cheaper one, which is how chiplets became normal. Zen 3 in 2020 unified eight cores into one cache domain and gained about 19% IPC; Zen 4 in 2022 moved to 5 nm, DDR5, PCIe 5 and AVX-512; Zen 5 in 2024 widened the front end again. The 3D V-Cache parts, from 2022, stack 64 MB of L3 on top of the compute die and turn cache capacity into frame rate. The node problem For thirty years, each process generation made transistors smaller, faster and lower-power at the same voltage. That pattern — Dennard scaling — ended around 2005. Leakage current stopped shrinking with the feature size, so a smaller transistor no longer meant a cooler one, and the 90 nm generation is where desktop cooling became a product category. Period Node Consequence 1985–1993 1.5 to 0.8 µm Frequency and features grew together 1997–2003 350 to 130 nm Clocks into the gigahertz, heat still manageable 2004–2006 90 to 65 nm Leakage, dual cores, the end of easy frequency 2008–2014 45 to 22 nm Turbo, integrated memory, power as the design target 2015–2019 14 to 7 nm A long pause, then chiplets and EUV 2020–2025 5 to 3 nm Stacked cache, tiles, and names that no longer compare The names themselves stopped being comparable: Intel's "Intel 7" and a foundry's "N7" are different densities and different yields. What matters to a buyer is the same as ever — performance in a specific workload, at a specific power limit — and the marketing number is the least useful input to that question. Hybrid cores Phones had shipped big.LITTLE for years before the desktop noticed. Lakefield in 2020 put one performance core and four efficiency cores on a package with stacked memory, mostly as a proof of concept. Alder Lake in 2021 made it mainstream: eight performance cores with SMT, eight efficiency cores without, and a hardware thread director telling the scheduler where each thread belongs. Raptor Lake added more efficiency cores; Arrow Lake dropped SMT and moved more of the chip into separate tiles. The trade is real. Efficiency cores are excellent at background work and terrible at a single heavy thread, so the operating system's placement decisions now matter as much as the core design. Tile-based packages — compute, graphics, SoC, I/O on separate dies, joined by a fast interconnect — let each part use the best node for its job, which is why a modern laptop chip can mix a 3 nm compute tile with older, cheaper support silicon. Virtualisation inherits the same complexity: the hypervisor has to describe a heterogeneous machine to guests that were written for a uniform one. Beside x86 ARM started in 1985 as a 32-bit RISC design with 25,000 transistors, and spent two decades inside phones before it threatened the laptop. M1 in 2020 is the moment the argument became practical: 16 billion transistors at 5 nm, unified memory shared by CPU and GPU, and performance per watt that x86 laptops could not match. M2, M3 and M4 followed on tighter nodes, and the same ISA now runs Windows laptops and cloud servers. RISC-V began at Berkeley in 2010 as a teaching ISA and became an open standard anyone can implement without a licence. It is already in microcontrollers and phone helper cores, and its base specification was ratified in 2019. Whether it reaches the desktop is a business question, not a technical one: the instruction set is free, but the compilers, the operating systems and the software ecosystem are not. What x86 keeps is the installed base. Every binary, every driver, every game and every piece of enterprise software written in the last forty years runs on it, and that is a moat no benchmark closes in a year. Security as silicon Features that used to be software became instructions. The NX bit arrived in 2004 to mark memory non-executable; VT-x and AMD-V in 2005 and 2006 made virtual machines practical; AES-NI in 2010 made disk encryption nearly free. Spectre and Meltdown, published in January 2018, showed that speculative execution itself leaks: a processor that guesses correctly still leaves traces, and an attacker who can time memory access can read them. The fixes — page-table isolation, microcode, compiler barriers — cost measurable performance, and some of them are still being tuned. The current generation ships confidential-computing modes (SGX, TDX, SEV) that encrypt a guest's memory from the hypervisor, and each new side-channel paper is followed by another round of firmware. The practical lesson for an operator is that a processor is now part of the attack surface: keeping microcode current matters as much as patching the compiling toolchain, and a benchmark that ignores mitigations is not measuring the machine you actually run. Reading the numbers The specification sheet is a set of trade-offs disguised as a list of features. Spec What it means Where it misleads Cores / threads Independent instruction streams; SMT doubles threads per core SMT adds much less than a second core on most workloads Base / boost clock Guaranteed and opportunistic frequency Boost is limited by heat, power and how many cores are busy L1 / L2 / L3 Latency hiding, from tens of kilobytes to tens of megabytes Capacity without bandwidth helps less than the number suggests TDP / PL1 / PL2 Cooling class and short-term power ceiling Two chips with the same TDP can differ by 50 W in practice Process node Density and efficiency class Names from different foundries are not comparable IPC Work per cycle for a given instruction mix It is workload-specific, not a universal score For choosing hardware, the order that survives contact with reality is: measure your own workload, then check power under sustained load, then check memory channels and cache, then look at the clock. A 65 W part that holds its boost beats a 125 W part that throttles after ninety seconds, and a chip with two memory channels will lose to one with four on anything that streams data. 2025–2026: what just landed Two years that answered the questions the roadmap had been asking since 2021: whether Intel could manufacture on its own leading node, whether AMD would take 2 nm to servers before desktops, and whether ARM laptops would survive their first generation. Intel: 18A arrives At CES 2026 Intel launched Core Ultra Series 3, codenamed Panther Lake — the first client system-on-chip built on Intel 18A, the 2 nm-class node with gate-all-around transistors and power delivery from the back of the wafer. The launch parts pair up to sixteen performance and efficiency cores with Xe3 graphics and a fifth-generation NPU, and the platform number Intel quotes reaches 180 TOPS once the GPU is counted. Pre-orders opened the day of the announcement, retail followed on 27 January, and Intel-powered Googlebook laptops from Acer, ASUS and Lenovo were announced in September for October availability. Wildcat Lake, the cost-optimised 18A part, sold out as demand outran supply, and Xeon 6+ — Clearwater Forest — became the first 18A server product in the first half of the year. Two details matter more than the benchmarks. 18A-P entered risk production on schedule and Nova Lake, the first client product on that refinement, is being lined up for CES 2027. And 18A capacity is now rationed: the company said it would convert some Oregon 18A wafer capacity to Intel 3 for Xeon, a change expected in the second half of 2027, because AI demand pays better than laptops. A process node is a business allocation, not a technical constant. AMD: Zen 6 goes server-first AMD shipped Zen 6 in July 2026 as EPYC 9006, codenamed Venice, and did it on TSMC's 2 nm process — the first high-performance part in the industry to ramp there. A socket holds up to 96 Zen 6 cores or 256 of the denser Zen 6c cores, with SP7 offering sixteen DDR5 channels at up to 12,800 MT/s and SP8 trading memory capacity for 128 PCIe 6.0 lanes; the top TDP is 600 watts. Venice-X, with stacked L3 reaching 1,152 MB per socket, and Verano, which integrates LPDDR, are 2027 parts. The ordering is the story. The new core reached servers first, where a socket competes on cores and memory bandwidth, and desktop Ryzen on Zen 6 had not shipped as of this writing. For a buyer that means the 2026 desktop is still the previous generation, and the interesting silicon is in the rack. ARM laptops stop being an experiment Apple's M5 arrived in October 2025 on a third-generation 3 nm process: nine or ten cores, 153 GB/s of unified memory bandwidth, and a Neural Engine that is no longer the only place AI runs, because the GPU gained accelerators of its own. Pro and Max versions followed through 2026, with the Ultra reaching the Mac Studio. Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Elite, announced in September 2025, puts up to eighteen Oryon cores at 5.0 GHz, 53 MB of cache and 228 GB/s of LPDDR5X into Windows laptops that shipped across 2026, and Nvidia's N1X added a third Arm supplier with twenty cores and a large integrated GPU. None of this retired x86. It changed the question a laptop buyer asks: not "which x86 core" but "which instruction set runs the software I need, at what power". For most people the answer is still x86, because the software is; the gap is now measured in battery hours, not compatibility. What did not happen No mainstream part reached 6 GHz. No desktop Zen 6 shipped in 2026. 2 nm did not arrive in a laptop first, because wafer cost and AI demand put server silicon ahead of client silicon. And the node names kept drifting: 18A, N2, N3P and "Intel 7" describe densities that cannot be compared across foundries, which is why this page keeps returning to the same advice — measure the workload, not the label. Where 2026 stands The line has settled into three lanes. Desktop x86 is on Zen 5 and Arrow Lake and is waiting for the next desktop cores, while the server parts lead the roadmap. Laptops are the contested ground, with Intel's own node finally shipping and three ARM vendors selling Windows machines. Embedded is quietly RISC-V's territory. Nothing about choosing hardware changed in the last two years: measure your own workload, check sustained power, then memory channels and cache, and look at the clock last. What changed is which logo is on the box, and how much of the performance now arrives through a scheduler deciding which core a thread belongs on. Forty-one years after the 386, the loop inside the chip is recognisably the same loop: fetch, decode, execute, retire. What changed is everything around it — how many copies run at once, where the memory lives, how the heat leaves, and how much of the design is now a bet on software that has not been written yet. No process is totally isolated while it shares a kernel or a hypervisor with an attacker. What you can build is a sealed cell : one application, one identity, one read-only root, one narrow data path, one network exception, one log stream — and a tested way back. This manual walks from first login to that cell, then shows you where the cell can still leak. Start at zero → Jump to the cell 14 chapters 60+ commands — sources 0 external assets HOST · DEBIAN 13 VM / HYPERVISOR BOUNDARY NAMESPACES · CGROUPS · LSM APP · UID 1001 CELL one job / no ambient authority systemd 257 AppArmor nftables cgroups v2 rootless Podman QEMU/KVM seccomp 00 Level 00 · Orientation · 12 min Field briefing # Isolation is not a product you install. It is a set of boundaries you can name, test and explain. Before you copy a single systemd directive, decide what you are isolating the application from , and what the application must still be able to reach. That answer decides the architecture. ! “Totally isolated” is a direction, not a checkbox. A container shares the host kernel. A VM shares the hypervisor. A separate host shares the network and the supply chain. Every layer removes a class of reachability; none removes the need to patch, monitor and recover. The three questions ask these before every directive What can it read? Configuration, credentials, other users' homes, the host's process list, kernel interfaces, the network. Confidentiality What can it write? Its data directory, logs, temporary files, the package database, cron, systemd units, other processes' memory. Integrity What can it reach? Loopback services, the LAN, the internet, the container runtime socket, the D-Bus, the kernel attack surface. Reachability Threat model, without theatre Write down the adversary and the boundary that is supposed to stop it. If the boundary is “the application is well behaved”, you do not have a boundary. The table below is a starting point, not a compliance claim. Adversary Typical entry Boundary that matters What usually fails Compromised dependency Build script, package, npm/pip crate, plugin Dedicated UID + read-only root + egress deny It runs with the app's full data and network reach Remote attacker Exposed service, weak auth, deserialisation Default-deny firewall + minimal service + patch cadence One forgotten port, one shared admin password Malicious local user Shell on the host, stolen key, sudo mistake Unix permissions + namespaces + audit trail World-writable paths, broad sudo, readable secrets Insider / operator error Wrong mount, copied unit, chmod 777 Immutable infrastructure + review + backups “Temporary” exceptions that never expire Kernel or hypervisor exploit Container escape, bug in a shared subsystem VM boundary + patched kernel + least privilege Assuming a container is a security boundary Supply-chain host Compromised mirror, image, update channel Signed packages + digest pinning + offline verification Blind curl | bash and floating tags The isolation ladder interactive Each rung is a real boundary with a real cost. Most production cells sit at rung 2 or 3; a hostile workload belongs at rung 4 or 5. Click a rung to see what it buys, what it costs, and where it still leaks. The cell contract seven properties One application One primary process, one job. No shell, no package manager, no compiler, no second daemon unless it is part of the same trust boundary. One identity A dedicated system UID/GID. No shared www-data or docker group. No sudo. No login shell. One writable path State lives in one directory. The root filesystem is read-only. Temporary files die with the process. One network story No network, loopback only, or a named egress path. “It needs internet” is not an architecture. One log stream stdout/stderr to journald, or one log directory collected by the host. The cell cannot rewrite history elsewhere. One update path Packages from Debian, images pinned by digest, or a rebuilt artifact. No self-updating binary inside the cell. One recovery path A snapshot, a backup, or a rebuild recipe that has been tested. If you cannot restore it, you do not own it. Ten rules that survive fashion Least privilege is a budget. Every permission you grant is a future exploit primitive. Start at zero, add one at a time, write down why. Deny by default. Firewall, filesystem, network families, capabilities, syscalls. Allow lists are shorter to review than deny lists. Read-only by default. A writable root is persistence. A writable data directory is the only thing that should survive a restart. No ambient authority. Environment variables, inherited file descriptors, D-Bus, the runtime socket and the host's SSH agent are all ambient authority. Secrets are files, not flags. Not in ExecStart= , not in Environment= , not in the image layer, not in shell history. The kernel is shared until it is not. Containers are excellent packaging and good isolation, but they are not a VM boundary. Patch the boundary, not only the app. Kernel, systemd, OpenSSH, the container runtime, the hypervisor, the firmware. Logs leave the cell. A compromised cell must not be able to edit the evidence of its own compromise. Test the failure. Kill the service, fill the disk, remove the network, reboot the host. Isolation that only works on the happy path is decoration. Write the exception down. Every ProtectHome=no or --privileged needs an owner, a reason and an expiry date. 01 Level 01 · Access · 18 min First login # The first hour decides whether the next year is recoverable. Install less, encrypt the disk, keep a console session open, create a named administrator, and make the baseline visible before you change anything. “Root and a password” is not an access design. Before the first prompt installer decisions Minimal, no desktop For a server cell, install the base system and OpenSSH only. Every extra package is another update stream and another parser exposed to the network. Encrypted root LUKS protects data at rest. It does not protect a running system. Keep a recovery key offline and test a boot with it. One admin identity Do not log in as root. Create an operator account, give it sudo, and use a key. Root gets no SSH and no shared password. Console access Know how to reach the VM console or the physical TTY before you touch SSH or nftables. A firewall mistake should not require a rescue ISO. First five commands look before touching hostnamectl ip -brief address ip route ss -tulpn systemctl --failed journalctl -p 3 -b --no-pager Read the output. You are looking for: a hostname you recognise, only the addresses you expect, no unexpected listeners, no failed units, and no repeating error at boot. Save that output; it is your first baseline. Create the operator not root adduser ops usermod -aG sudo ops install -d -m 0700 -o ops -g ops /home/ops/.ssh # On your workstation: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100 -C "ops@workstation" ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ops@server.example.test # Test the new session before closing the old one: ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey ops@server.example.test ! Keep the old session open. Open a second terminal, log in with the key, run sudo -v , then close nothing until the new path is proven. Most “SSH locked me out” stories start with a single session and a reload. Harden SSH without guessing drop-in config Debian reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the files in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ . Put local policy in a numbered drop-in so package updates do not fight your edits. sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF' PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PubkeyAuthentication yes AuthenticationMethods publickey AllowUsers ops X11Forwarding no AllowAgentForwarding no AllowTcpForwarding no PermitTunnel no GatewayPorts no MaxAuthTries 3 MaxSessions 2 LoginGraceTime 20 ClientAliveInterval 300 ClientAliveCountMax 2 LogLevel VERBOSE EOF sudo sshd -t sudo systemctl reload ssh sudo sshd -T | grep -E 'permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|allowusers|maxauthtries' Directive Why What it breaks PermitRootLogin no Removes a known username with unlimited authority from the network. Root-only workflows; use ops + sudo instead. PasswordAuthentication no Passwords are guessable, replayable and shared. Keys are not immortal, but they are auditable. Old clients, emergency access if the key is lost — keep a console path. AllowUsers ops Reduces the account surface even if another user is created later. Automation accounts; add them explicitly or use AllowGroups . AllowTcpForwarding no Stops an SSH account from becoming a general-purpose proxy into the network. Legitimate tunnels; use a dedicated bastion if required. MaxAuthTries 3 Reduces online guessing and noisy logs. Nothing important if keys are used. Sudo, with a paper trail sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-ops # ops ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL # Defaults:ops use_pty # Defaults:ops logfile="/var/log/sudo-ops.log" sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-ops sudo visudo -c use_pty prevents a simple background process from surviving the sudo session. The logfile is a second copy of intent; keep it on the host, not inside the cell. Patch and make it automatic sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade sudo apt install --no-install-recommends unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges needrestart sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades # Confirm the timer and the effective policy: systemctl status unattended-upgrades --no-pager sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | tail -40 i Automatic updates are not automatic safety. They need a reboot for kernel and some library changes, a working mirror, and a rollback plan. needrestart tells you which services still run old libraries; it does not restart them for you unless configured. Write the baseline evidence before opinion sudo install -d -m 0700 /root/baseline { date -u hostnamectl uname -a dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n' ss -tulpn nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null || true systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled --no-pager } | sudo tee "/root/baseline/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt" >/dev/null sudo chmod 0600 /root/baseline/*.txt ls -l /root/baseline Time, DNS and the network story timedatectl set-ntp true timedatectl status resolvectl status # What is this host allowed to reach? Write it down. ip -brief address ip route sudo ss -tulpn Time matters because TLS, logs and audit correlation depend on it. DNS matters because “no network” is a lie if the resolver still leaks queries. Decide both before you build the cell. 02 Level 02 · Operations · 20 min Command survival kit # You do not need five hundred commands. You need twenty that answer four questions: who am I , what is running , what can it reach , and what changed . Everything else is a variation on those. Identity id , getent passwd , getent group , sudo -l , loginctl list-sessions . who Process ps auxf , pstree -ap , systemd-cgls , lsof -p , /proc/<pid>/ . what Reach ss -tulpn , ip route , nft list ruleset , resolvectl status , lsns . where Change journalctl , apt history , dpkg -V , debsums -c , systemctl status . when Packages: know what you installed apt update apt full-upgrade apt policy openssh-server apt list --installed apt-mark showmanual # Which package owns this file? What did this package install? dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd dpkg -L openssh-server # Has any file changed since the package was installed? dpkg -V openssh-server debsums -c Task Command Note Full upgrade apt full-upgrade May remove packages; read the plan before saying yes. Why is this installed? apt-mark showmanual Manual packages are your real dependency budget. Pin a version apt-mark hold pkg Debt. Record the reason and a review date. Find config files dpkg-query -W -f='${Conffiles}\n' pkg Useful before editing a package's default. Integrity check dpkg -V Compares installed files with package metadata. Security tracker debsecan --suite trixie Needs network access to fetch data. systemd: the control plane systemctl status cell.service --no-pager systemctl start cell.service systemctl enable --now cell.service systemctl restart cell.service systemctl reload-or-restart cell.service systemctl cat cell.service systemctl edit --full cell.service systemctl daemon-reload systemctl show cell.service -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p NoNewPrivileges systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled systemctl --failed systemctl cat shows the unit and its drop-ins in the order systemd reads them. When a directive “does not work”, the usual cause is a later drop-in overriding it. systemctl show is the truth, not the file you remember editing. Logs: read the timeline, not the last line journalctl -u cell.service -f journalctl -u cell.service --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager journalctl -p warning -b --no-pager journalctl -p err..alert --since today --no-pager journalctl -k -b --no-pager journalctl --disk-usage journalctl --verify journalctl -o json-pretty -u cell.service -n 1 i Boot IDs are your friend. -b means this boot, -b -1 the previous one. After a crash, compare journalctl -b -1 -p err with the current boot before you reboot again and destroy the evidence. Network and namespaces: what is actually listening ss -tulpn ss -tan state established ip -brief address ip route ip netns list lsns resolvectl status # Enter a process's network namespace (requires privilege): sudo nsenter -t "$(pgrep -x cell)" -n ss -tulpn Files and privilege: the two audits you run first # Setuid and setgid binaries: a short list is a good list. sudo find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -print # World-writable files and directories without the sticky bit. sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print sudo find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 -print # File capabilities instead of setuid. sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null # Who can sudo, and to what? sudo -l getent group sudo getent group wheel ! Every setuid binary is a small root door. Remove what you do not use, prefer file capabilities with a narrow capability, and never “fix” a permission problem with chmod 777 . A world-writable directory is a place to plant a symlink, a library or a unit file. Things not to do the short list curl … | bash — you are executing a moving target with your privileges. Download, verify a signature or hash, read it, then run it. chmod -R 777 — it turns a permission bug into a persistence mechanism. Copy-paste a unit with --privileged — you have disabled most of the boundaries you are trying to build. Mount the container runtime socket into an untrusted container — that is root on the host with extra steps. Run a database as root — there is no recovery benefit, only a larger blast radius. Expose a service “just for a minute” — scanners do not wait for you to close it. 03 Level 03 · Advanced foundations · 28 min Isolation primitives # The Linux kernel already contains the fences: identities, capabilities, namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and Linux Security Modules. systemd, Podman, bubblewrap and Firejail are different ways to ask the kernel for the same fences. Learn the primitives and the tools stop being magic. The six layers name the boundary Layer Question Primitive Typical tool Identity Who is this process? UID, GID, supplementary groups, capabilities useradd , setpriv , capsh Filesystem What can it see and write? Umas são verdadeiras, outras são equívocos, algumas são instrumentais — alguém a usar a polícia para resolver uma disputa privada. O trabalho começa exactamente onde a intuição falha: em decidir quem merece atenção, quanto dessa atenção é legítima e que indício sobrevive a uma verificação honesta. A tentação é tratar isto como uma questão de carácter: «bons polícias vêem quem é culpado». Não é. É uma questão de desenho de processo — de probabilidades, de sequências, de verificação independente e de limites. E, ao contrário do que o cinema sugere, a maior parte dos erros graves não nasce de maldade. Nasce de um método que nunca foi testado contra a hipótese de o suspeito ser inocente. 0.1 Duas perguntas que parecem a mesma Quase todos os erros de investigação começam numa inversão silenciosa de duas perguntas: Pergunta A — a que interessa ao tribunal P(culpado | indício) Dado este vestígio, este comportamento, esta coincidência, qual é a probabilidade de esta pessoa ter cometido o crime? Podem diferir por ordens de grandeza. Confundi-los é o erro estatístico mais frequente em processos penais — e não é um detalhe académico: foi suficiente para condenar pessoas que nunca tinham estado perto do crime. «O perito disse que só uma em cada milhão de pessoas teria este perfil. Nenhum exige um polícia corrupto. Todos exigem apenas pressão e um processo mal desenhado. 1. Taxa-base ignorada Um indício raro entre inocentes continua a ser comum quando os inocentes são milhões. 2. Visão em túnel A hipótese inicial passa a filtrar o que se recolhe — e o que se descarta. 3. Prova contaminada A expectativa do investigador molda a interpretação do perito, da testemunha e do próprio registo. 4. Confissão fabricada Sob isolamento, exaustão e sugestão, pessoas inocentes confessam — e depois não conseguem desdizer-se. 5. Pressão para fechar Um caso por resolver é um problema institucional; um caso fechado, mesmo errado, parece uma solução. 6. Métricas perversas Se o sucesso é medido por detenções e não por decisões correctas, o sistema aprende a deter mais. 0.4 Nenhuma polícia está imune Este manual usa casos reais de oito países. Nenhum deles é uma acusação a um povo, a uma farda ou a uma nação. É exactamente o contrário: as más decisões são tratadas aqui como iguais entre si — portuguesas, francesas, britânicas, italianas, neerlandesas, espanholas, norte-americanas ou japonesas. O que muda é o enquadramento legal e a cultura institucional; o que se repete é a arquitectura do erro. A intuição humana trata probabilidades como se fossem opiniões: «é muito provável» quer dizer «estou convencido». O raciocínio probatório exige outra coisa — números que se podem confrontar, taxas que se podem medir e a humildade de perguntar «comparado com o quê?». 1.1 A inversão que arruína inquéritos Um laboratório conclui: «a probabilidade de encontrar este ADN ao acaso é de uma em um milhão». Um relatório policial escreve: «há uma probabilidade de 99,9999 % de o suspeito ser culpado». A segunda frase não decorre da primeira. Falta a taxa-base: quantas pessoas poderiam ter deixado aquele vestígio, e com que frequência este tipo de vestígio aparece em transferências indirectas. Em 1999, no Reino Unido, a pediatra Roy Meadow testemunhou que a probabilidade de duas mortes súbitas numa família «boa» era de uma em 73 milhões. A estatística foi tratada como prova de homicídio. Sally Clark foi condenada; a condenação foi anulada em 2003, depois de a Royal Statistical Society ter criticado publicamente o raciocínio. O erro não estava na peritagem médica sobre as mortes: estava na aritmética do tribunal. Regra operacional Nunca converter um resultado pericial em probabilidade de culpa sem três elementos: a taxa-base da população relevante, a probabilidade de o vestígio aparecer por outra via e a probabilidade de o vestígio não aparecer se a pessoa for culpada . Sem os três, o número é retórica, não prova. 1.2 Sensibilidade, especificidade e o número que falta Qualquer teste — um cão detector, um algoritmo de reconhecimento facial, um agente experiente, um exame de ADN — tem duas qualidades mensuráveis: Sensibilidade (detecção): de todos os culpados, quantos são assinalados. Especificidade : de todos os inocentes, quantos não são assinalados. Nenhuma das duas responde à pergunta do investigador. A que responde é o valor preditivo positivo (VPP): dos assinalados, quantos são realmente culpados. E o VPP depende de algo que o teste não controla: a prevalência do fenómeno na população em que é aplicado. É por isso que o mesmo teste é aceitável numa fronteira e inaceitável numa escola. Consequência prática Se a sua unidade detém 60 pessoas com base num indicador com VPP de 15 %, está a produzir cerca de 51 detenções de inocentes por 9 de culpados. A resposta correcta não é abandonar o indicador: é usá-lo para priorizar verificação, nunca para fundamentar detenção , e medir o VPP em cada contexto antes de o escalar. 1.3 O limiar: onde se corta o sinal Nenhum indicador separa o mundo em dois. O que existe é uma distribuição de comportamentos, vestígios ou pontuações — e um limiar escolhido por alguém. Baixar o limiar aumenta a detecção e multiplica os falsos positivos; subir o limiar poupa inocentes e deixa passar culpados. A decisão é política e ética antes de ser técnica, e deve ser registada como tal. 1.4 O rácio de verosimilhança: a linguagem honesta da prova A forma mais robusta de comunicar o peso de uma prova é o rácio de verosimilhança (LR). Não diz «a probabilidade de culpa é X». Diz quanto é que a prova desloca a balança entre duas hipóteses: LR = P(prova | hipótese da acusação) ÷ P(prova | hipótese da defesa) Um LR de 10 significa: a prova é dez vezes mais provável se a acusação for verdadeira. Não significa que a acusação seja dez vezes mais provável — para isso é preciso combinar o LR com a probabilidade a priori (probabilidade prévia), que é exactamente o que a falácia do Ministério Público ignora. A escala verbal abaixo é a usada, com variantes, em guias forenses europeus; serve para comunicar, não para substituir o número. Escala verbal de interpretação de um rácio de verosimilhança LR Leitura O que ainda não foi dito 1 Neutro A prova não distingue as hipóteses. 2 – 10 Fraco a moderado Pode ser compatível com várias explicações inocentes. 10 – 100 Moderado a forte Exige verificação independente e controlo de transferência. 100 – 1 000 Forte Só é interpretável com dados populacionais válidos para o contexto. > 1 000 Muito forte Continua a não ser uma probabilidade de culpa. 1.5 Quantos indícios fazem uma prova? A tentação é somar indícios fracos: «cinco coincidências, cada uma com 20 % de probabilidade, dão 67 %». Isto só é verdade se as coincidências forem independentes — e, numa investigação, quase nunca são. Se o mesmo polícia recolheu os cinco elementos, se a mesma testemunha os referiu, se todos derivam da mesma conversa ouvida na mesma noite, então não há cinco provas: há uma prova contada cinco vezes. Teste de dependência Para cada par de indícios, pergunte: «se eu soubesse que o primeiro é falso, a probabilidade do segundo mudaria?» Se a resposta for sim, os indícios estão correlacionados. Nesse caso, some com cautela — ou melhor, procure uma fonte independente que não tenha sido exposta à hipótese inicial. 1.6 O que a probabilidade não decide Mesmo uma probabilidade bem calculada não condena ninguém. Em Portugal, a presunção de inocência está consagrada no artigo 32.º, n.º 2, da Constituição, e o processo penal assenta no princípio in dubio pro reo : a dúvida razoável resolve-se a favor do arguido. O padrão não é «mais provável que não»; é «certeza para além da dúvida razoável», avaliada em conjunto e sujeita a contraditório. Isto significa que o trabalho policial pode — e deve — produzir probabilidades, hierarquias de hipóteses e rácios. O que não pode é confundir a sua própria escala interna de suspeita com o padrão jurídico de prova. A fronteira entre as duas é o que separa uma investigação de uma convicção. Um polícia experiente «sente» quando algo não bate certo. Esse sentir é real e tem valor — mas é matéria-prima, não conclusão. A análise criminal existe para transformar intuições em hipóteses testáveis sobre onde , quando e como o crime acontece, antes de as transformar em suspeitas sobre quem . 2.1 Indicadores: o que um sinal prova (e o que não prova) Chamamos indicador a uma característica observável que aumenta a probabilidade de um determinado tipo de crime naquele contexto . Um indicador não é um diagnóstico. Nervosismo, por exemplo, é mais frequente em pessoas que já foram maltratadas pela polícia, em pessoas com perturbação de ansiedade e em pessoas com pressa do que em criminosos — e é por isso que não pode fundamentar sozinho uma revista. São um aviso: cada sinal tem de ser ligado a um crime concreto, num local concreto, com um guião concreto . É essa ligação — e não a aparência — que pode justificar uma abordagem proporcional. 2.2 Concentração: o crime não é uniforme O crime concentra-se. Uma minoria de locais produz a maioria dos incidentes; uma minoria de vítimas sofre a maioria das repetições; e, após um crime, a probabilidade de novo crime no mesmo local e nas semanas seguintes sobe — fenómeno designado near-repeat victimisation . Isto não é uma teoria sobre pessoas: é uma regularidade sobre lugares e tempo, e é testável. A experiência de Minneapolis (1995) é o marco: 110 pontos quentes foram aleatorizados; em 55 deles a patrulha visível foi duplicada. As chamadas por crime caíram 6 a 13 % nos locais tratados e a desordem observada foi cerca de metade da dos locais de controlo. Revisões sistemáticas posteriores encontraram efeitos consistentes, geralmente pequenos, sem deslocação relevante do crime para áreas vizinhas e com indícios de difusão de benefícios. 2.3 O teste de resultado: detectar discriminação sem ler intenções Como saber se uma prática é injusta sem interrogar consciências? Há um teste estatístico simples e exigente: comparar, entre grupos, a taxa de resultado das mesmas acções. Se 10 000 paragens de um grupo produzem 8 % de resultados positivos e 10 000 paragens de outro produzem 20 %, há duas hipóteses: ou o critério de paragem é diferente, ou o mesmo critério é aplicado a pessoas diferentes. Nenhuma delas se resolve com boas intenções. Em Inglaterra e no País de Gales, no ano terminado em Março de 2025, a taxa de revistas de pessoas negras foi 3,8 vezes superior à de pessoas brancas. Isto não prova, por si só, discriminação em cada abordagem: a polícia é destacada de forma desigual e o crime não se distribui ao acaso. Mas obriga a uma pergunta de auditoria — e a resposta não pode ser «os números não dizem nada». Cuidado com a comparação simples Comparar taxas brutas entre grupos é o começo, não o fim. É preciso estratificar por local, hora, tipo de crime e critério de paragem. É precisamente aqui que aparece o paradoxo de Simpson: uma diferença que desaparece — ou se inverte — quando se olha para dentro dos estratos. 2.4 Redes: associação não é culpa A análise de ligações é uma das ferramentas mais úteis e mais mal utilizadas. Uma rede mostra quem contacta quem, quem co-reside, quem partilha meios — e ajuda a identificar papéis : quem fornece, quem transporta, quem guarda, quem vende. Mas a proximidade numa rede não é um facto criminoso. Estar no mesmo gráfico que um suspeito é tão incriminatório como estar na mesma cidade que ele. 2.5 Do dado à decisão: o ciclo de informação Em Portugal, como na maioria dos sistemas, a informação policial circula por um ciclo: orientação → recolha → processamento → análise → disseminação → acção → revisão . O elo mais frágil é quase sempre o último. Sem revisão, o ciclo não aprende: repete o mesmo erro com mais dados. Inteligência não é o mesmo que prova Inteligência Prova Orienta recursos e hipóteses.
